data.title: A rapamycin-sensitive signaling pathway contributes to long-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus
data.authors: Tang SJ; Reis G; Kang H; Gingras AC; Sonenberg N; Schuman EM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Rat and mouse hippocampal slices (field recordings, immunostaining); cultured rat hippocampal neurons; Western blot of rat hippocampus
data.finding: The authors showed that mTOR, 4E-BP1, 4E-BP2 and eIF4E are present in rat hippocampus and sit in dendrites, close to synapses, where their staining overlapped with the postsynaptic protein PSD-95. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin in hippocampal slices reduced late-phase long-term potentiation (LTP) after high-frequency stimulation, while early-phase LTP was unaffected. Rapamycin also blocked the synaptic potentiation induced by the growth factor BDNF. This was one of the early papers to tie a rapamycin-sensitive pathway to the protein-synthesis-dependent phase of synaptic plasticity and to suggest it controls local translation at synapses. Boundary: rodent brain slices and cultured neurons; mTOR targets were localised but their phosphorylation during LTP was not reported in the abstract; no behaviour or memory test.
data.abstract_excerpt: Many forms of long-lasting behavioral and synaptic plasticity require the synthesis of new proteins. For example, long-term potentiation (LTP) that endures for more than an hour requires both transcription and translation. The signal-transduction mechanisms that couple synaptic events to protein translational machinery during long-lasting synaptic plasticity, however, are not well understood.

extracted_findings.species: Rat; mouse (hippocampal slices and cultured neurons)
extracted_findings.effect: Rapamycin reduced late-phase LTP and blocked BDNF-induced potentiation; early LTP unchanged
